I was experimenting with having Novation control an Ableton Instrument such as Operator by using shift + Note to select channel 2 out, then putting the Operator instrument on the set's track 5 MIDI in, while also gating LPP→MF's MIDI out to channel 1, so the parts of the sequencer meant for the MicroFreak didn't get the cross-talk. It does bug me that I need to use the mic to say what preset I'm selecting. If only there was a way to use custom mode on the LPP to send sysex or patch set or preset select messages on the μF. Of course, I could literally do that, but I'd have a larger problem when it came to selection. I suppose there are "sliders" in Custom mode. It would likely be annoying to try to land on a known preset. I think the track indicators give me eight pages of custom modes. I suppose I could use some kind of automation to populate them. Maybe Page 2 could be pads I've used recently, 1 per line, with a binary representation of the preset number. If I have any illuminated button on a row sending that preset's sysex, I can use 2⁸ in binary presets, which is almost enough at 256. I would prefer 2⁹ or 512, that would put me over the μF's limit. maybe I could drop the least significant bit. Or I could use color for a few more bits. Then again, doing mental binary during a live performance sounds like a stupid plan. If I was streaming / recording from above, it could detect the preset.

A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack is when an attacker secretly positions themselves between two parties and intercepts their communication.
Conceptually, it breaks trust in the channel rather than necessarily breaking the app itself.
Common outcomes include eavesdropping, message tampering, credential theft, or session hijacking when integrity and authenticity checks are weak or absent.

Short answer: man finds and formats a manual page, then hands the result to a pager. The macOS man program and its usual pager, less, do not expose the page's headings as a navigable hierarchy. Neovim's built-in man-page viewer does: open the page with :Man tmux, then press gO for a table of contents.

Can I browse man pages by heading, including in nvim or LazyVim?

The installed /usr/bin/man accepts -P pager; MANPAGER overrides PAGER. Its default is less, whose navigation is text-based: search for an uppercase heading with /^COMMANDS$, then use n and N to move among matches. A broader search such as /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9 /_-]*$ finds many top-level headings. less does not parse those matches into an outline. Answer/Official from OpenBSD man(1) and less(1).

Djot is a light markup syntax. It derives most of its features from commonmark, but it fixes a few things that make commonmark's syntax complex and difficult to parse efficiently. It is also much fuller-featured than commonmark, with support for definition lists, footnotes, tables, several new kinds of inline formatting (insert, delete, highlight, superscript, subscript), math, smart punctuation, attributes that can be applied to any element, and generic containers for block-level, inline-level, and raw content. The project began as an attempt to implement some of the ideas I suggested in Beyond Markdown.

When helping engineers with technical tasks, LLM based AI Agents need to be able to communicate architectural ideas to both humans and other agents. Currently, LLMs can produce Mermaid Diagram in Mermaid, but the only way to render that is to call Mermaid/mmdc, a CLI tool which actually, according to Mermaid/DeepWiki, uses , a Browser/Headless, to render the image.
Diagramming is an afterthought in every programming language
As a result, cannot compile to verify the syntax of the mermaid diagrams it generates, as it only has access to a python interpreter with mostly Native Implementation libraries.

Instead, we should create a language specification for a text to diagram markup language which is intended to produce Native Implementations of the rendering behavior in each target language using AI Coding.

Create a library which facilitates creating a spec that expresses expected formatting for a given structured language. The library should have an opinionated way to create a clear spec and include LLM-powered tools to create such a spec using a requirements elicitation process. The spec should format contain example artifacts which can aid in few-shot prompting. The library should enable compiling such a spec into an LLM-powered application which starts out just using the LLM to directly format the instructions in a prompted way. Over time, the prompted LLM-powered application should start to write code to automate the process and built up syntax parsing approaches, adding the approach to a memory bank that it can draw upon to make the conversion approach more consistent and tested.

Modern workflows that involve AI-generated or collaboratively edited Markdown often encounter issues with table alignment and the integrity of fenced code blocks—especially when code blocks embed Markdown. To address these consistently, the ideal solution is a fast, established CLI tool (preferably Rust-based) capable of robustly formatting Markdown for both human and machine readability, easy integration into pre-commit hooks, and seamless operation in CI/CD environments. This report evaluates leading tools, compares their strengths for the stated requirements, and provides practical configuration examples.
